canonical_statement: The article reports expert opinions and recommendations intended to optimize CKD screening and management in people with diabetes and to provide practical, simplified algorithms for primary care clinicians.
The authors recommend early and regular CKD screening in people with T2D using both eGFR and UACR.
The authors recommend reviewing CKD risk with the KDIGO heatmap at least annually to optimize treatment and slow CKD progression.
The authors describe lifestyle modification as the foundation of CKD risk reduction in people with T2D.
The authors recommend a four-pillar pharmacotherapy approach using RAS inhibition, an SGLT2 inhibitor, finerenone, and a GLP-1 receptor agonist for people with CKD and T2D.
The CardioRenal Initiative meeting was held on 20-21 October 2023 in Montreal, Canada, with support from Bayer.
The meeting included 40 experts in nephrology, cardiology, diabetology/endocrinology, and primary care from Europe, North America, and Asia.
A primary care advisory board workshop discussed optimal management of CKD associated with T2D and proposed screening, monitoring, and treatment algorithms.
The workshop discussion included an analysis of major international recommendations from the ADA, KDIGO, and ESC.
Genetic predisposition and genetic testing were not discussed during the CardioRenal Initiative meeting and were outside the article's main scope.
The article states that supplementary material is available online at DOI 10.2337/figshare.29260568.
The review reports 2017 estimates of CKD prevalence at 9.1% of the global population, corresponding to 697.5 million cases and 1.2 million deaths.
The review reports a projection that CKD could become the fifth largest global cause of death by 2040.
The review reports that approximately 30-40% of people with diabetes have CKD.
The review reports that diabetes contributes to 47% of prevalent ESKD and 38% of incident ESKD.
The review reports that T2D increases cardiovascular disease risk two- to fourfold.
The review reports that cardiovascular death risk may be about threefold higher in people with CKD and T2D than in people with T2D without CKD.
The review reports that approximately 50% of people with stage 4 or 5 CKD have cardiovascular disease and that 40-50% of CKD-related deaths in advanced CKD are due to cardiovascular disease.

The review reports life-expectancy reductions at age 30 of 10.2 years in men and 11.7 years in women with diabetes alone, 5.7 and 6.7 years with CKD alone, and 11.5 and 14.1 years with both CKD and diabetes.
The review identifies therapeutic inertia as a key barrier to timely use of treatments that slow CKD progression and reduce cardiorenal risk.
The review states that primary care clinicians are positioned to support early CKD diagnosis, establish treatment regimens, monitor outcomes, and coordinate multidisciplinary care.
The review identifies frequent guideline updates, divergent recommendations, and guideline complexity as barriers to use in primary care.
The review uses the KDIGO CKD definition of abnormalities present for more than 3 months, including eGFR below 60 mL/min/1.73 m2 or one or more markers of kidney damage.

outcome.definition: Abnormalities of kidney structure or function present for more than 3 months, including eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m2 or markers of kidney damage.

canonical_statement: Albuminuria is identified as a marker of kidney damage at UACR at least 30 mg/g or at least 3 mg/mmol.

The screening algorithm identifies diabetes, hypertension, obesity, smoking, retinopathy, age over 60 years, erectile dysfunction, nephrotoxic drug exposure, sleep disorders, CKD or family history of CKD, cardiovascular disease, and heart failure as CKD risk indicators.

population.label: People with one or more listed CKD risk indicators

canonical_statement: At-risk individuals should be screened for both impaired kidney function and kidney damage by measuring eGFR and UACR.
The review describes eGFR as the overall measure of kidney excretory function and UACR as a sensitive early indicator of kidney damage.
At-risk individuals with eGFR at least 60 mL/min/1.73 m2 and UACR below 30 mg/g should be rescreened at least annually with eGFR, UACR, HbA1c, LDL cholesterol, and blood pressure assessment.
Individuals with eGFR below 60 mL/min/1.73 m2 or UACR at least 30 mg/g should be retested after 3 months, with blood pressure and glycemic treatment optimized between tests.
The screening algorithm calls for a confirmatory second test before diagnosing CKD and states that chronicity should not be based on a single abnormal eGFR or UACR result.
For a positive UACR below 20 mg/mmol, the Figure 1 footnote advises confirmation of two out of three positive results over at least 3 months.
Figure 1 prints a statement that UACR at least 20 mg/mol is indicative of diabetic nephropathy, despite using mg/mmol in the surrounding threshold text.
After CKD diagnosis, the authors recommend KDIGO heatmap risk stratification and treatment according to risk.
For people with T2D and CKD, eGFR, UACR, HbA1c, LDL cholesterol, and blood pressure should be assessed at least annually for life.
Individuals with high-risk or established CKD should be monitored more frequently than once yearly.
Individuals with stage 4 or 5 CKD should be referred to a nephrologist.
The review recommends semiquantitative or quantitative albuminuria screening as an initial test, followed by confirmation with a laboratory quantitative UACR test.
The review notes that semiquantitative UACR assessment could expand screening access in clinics without laboratory services and may support home screening.
Patient education should explain the distinction between kidney damage and kidney function, including the use of UACR to assess damage and eGFR to assess function.
Figure 2 uses KDIGO albuminuria categories A1 below 30 mg/g, A2 30-300 mg/g, and A3 above 300 mg/g, together with eGFR categories G1 through G5 to set monitoring and referral frequency.
Figure 1 lists KFRE, CKD-PC, and Klinrisk as examples of kidney risk calculators that can supplement KDIGO heatmap stratification.
The stated therapeutic goals are to reduce cardiovascular and heart failure risk, reduce CKD progression risk, and achieve adequate glycemic control to reduce morbidity and mortality.
Lifestyle management includes weight management, exercise, smoking reduction or cessation, dietary adjustment, and adequate sleep.
The review recommends optimizing HbA1c, hypertension, lipid abnormalities, heart failure, and sleep apnea as part of CKD management in T2D.
The four treatment pillars are RAS inhibition with an ACE inhibitor or ARB, an SGLT2 inhibitor, finerenone, and a GLP-1 receptor agonist, on a foundation of lifestyle modification.
People with CKD and T2D should receive an ACE inhibitor or ARB titrated to the maximum tolerated dose when indicated, with other pillars added as required.
An SGLT2 inhibitor with proven kidney or cardiovascular benefit is recommended for CKD in T2D when eGFR is at least 20 mL/min/1.73 m2.
The review states that KDIGO permits continuation of an SGLT2 inhibitor if eGFR falls below 20 mL/min/1.73 m2 after initiation.
The prose recommends finerenone 10 mg once daily when eGFR is greater than 25 to at most 60 mL/min/1.73 m2.

exposures.details: Prose eGFR criterion: >25 to <=60 mL/min/1.73 m2.

canonical_statement: The prose recommends finerenone 20 mg once daily when eGFR is at least 60 mL/min/1.73 m2.

The prose finerenone dose thresholds overlap at eGFR 60 mL/min/1.73 m2 because the 10 mg range is printed as greater than 25 to at most 60, while the 20 mg range begins at at least 60; Figure 5 instead prints greater than 25 to below 60 for 10 mg.
Figure 5 places finerenone use in people with eGFR at least 25 mL/min/1.73 m2, albuminuria at least 30 mg/g, and serum potassium at most 5.0 mmol/L.

exposures.details: Figure 5 eligibility: eGFR >=25 mL/min/1.73 m2, albuminuria >=30 mg/g, serum potassium <=5.0 mmol/L.

canonical_statement: Figure 5 recommends checking serum potassium and eGFR 4 weeks after finerenone initiation or dose adjustment and continuing periodic potassium monitoring.
Figure 5 places GLP-1 receptor agonist therapy in the CKD and T2D treatment pathway irrespective of glycemic control.

exposures.details: Use irrespective of glycemic control in Figure 5.

canonical_statement: Figure 5 suggests a dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker and/or diuretic when additional blood pressure lowering is needed and a steroidal MRA for resistant hypertension when eGFR is at least 45 mL/min/1.73 m2.
Figure 3 states that aspirin should be used only for secondary prevention, particularly in older populations.

Treatment selection should consider medication safety and tolerability, patient preferences, regimen convenience, long-term efficacy, and the individual's ability and willingness to follow a complex plan.

The authors state that despite limited guideline direction on simultaneous versus sequential initiation, patients should ideally receive all applicable treatment pillars in a timely manner if they tolerate them.
Figure 4 cautions about depression and suicidality with GLP-1 receptor agonists and describes an FDA cautionary approach current to the source.

Figure 5 displays an SGLT2 inhibitor branch using eGFR at least 20 mL/min/1.73 m2 together with albuminuria at least 200 mg/g, while the surrounding prose recommends SGLT2 inhibitor treatment for CKD in T2D at eGFR at least 20 without requiring that albuminuria threshold.

The review reports that only about one-third of people with T2D are tested for CKD within the first year after diabetes diagnosis.
The review reports that less than one-fourth of people with diabetes are aware of CKD risk and that up to 90% of people with CKD in the United States do not know they have CKD.
The review reports that only about 50% of people with chronic conditions, including CKD, adhere to long-term treatment strategies.
Table 1 groups low CKD screening into patient concerns, clinical prioritization, provider workload and beliefs, and health-system barriers such as lack of screening incentives and rigid protocols.
Table 1 attributes inadequate awareness of treatment recommendations to limited physician education opportunities and the complexity of frequently updated guidelines.
Table 1 attributes inadequate adherence to treatment recommendations to resistance to change, preference for familiar medications, overestimation of target attainment, and poor long-term adherence.
The authors propose routine UACR testing and inclusion of CKD screening in routine blood and urine panels for people with diabetes to support earlier diagnosis.
The authors recommend educating people with diabetes and other CKD risk conditions about their risk level and supporting self-management.
The authors state that a multidisciplinary primary care team may improve management of people with CKD and diabetes when such a team is available.
The authors suggest motivational interviewing as a possible adherence strategy while recognizing that financial limitations and lack of specialist access can constrain treatment adherence.
The review points to ADA clinician and patient infographics as potential shared visual tools for CKD awareness and clinician-patient communication.
The recommendations are based on the expert opinions of 40 specialists across nephrology, cardiology, diabetology/endocrinology, and primary care after review of ADA, KDIGO, and ESC guidance.
The authors state that their algorithms are deliberately simplified for primary care and are not as extensive as the full ADA, KDIGO, and ESC guidelines.
The authors state that current treatment guidelines do not yet recommend genetic screening or provide personalized-treatment algorithms for CKD and T2D.
The article states that Bayer AG supported the work; Bayer manufactures finerenone and sponsored FIDELIO-DKD and FIGARO-DKD.
Medical writing, editorial support, fact checking, referencing, formatting, proofreading, submission support, and figure preparation were supported by Bayer.

Eugene E. Wright reports speaker, advisory-board, and consulting relationships that include Bayer and several other diabetes and cardiovascular companies, and he is an associate editor of Clinical Diabetes.
Ana Cebrian reports advisory, lecture, and research relationships with multiple pharmaceutical companies.

Daniel Ngui reports advisory and speaking relationships that include Bayer and other companies, participation in FINE-REAL and Pioneer REAL research, and membership on guideline and education committees.
The authors conclude that CKD remains underrecognized and undertreated in people with T2D despite effective therapies that slow progression.
The authors conclude that CKD risk in people with T2D should be reviewed annually or more often according to stage, using eGFR, UACR, and KDIGO risk stratification to guide treatment.
The authors conclude that a lifestyle-based four-pillar pharmacotherapy approach should cover cardiovascular, kidney, and diabetes-related therapeutic goals.
The authors conclude that early detection, comprehensive management, patient education, and multidisciplinary care can slow CKD progression and reduce cardiovascular complications.
